did_you_know.text: Did you know? The Torah calls Nisan “the first month,” and the Tabernacle was set up on its first day. This was about a year after the Exodus.
Did you know? The curtain was more than a covering: it separated the Holy Place from the Holy of Holies, where the Ark of the Testimony stood.
Did you know? The menorah had seven branches and lamps, as described in the instructions for making it in chapter 25.
Did you know? The golden altar was used for incense, not for animal sacrifices. It stood inside the Tent of Meeting, near the curtain.
Did you know? The laver was a basin of water where the priests washed their hands and feet before performing their service.
Did you know? The anointing oil was a sacred mixture of olive oil and fragrant spices, and an identical mixture could not be used for ordinary purposes.
Did you know? The priesthood was meant to continue through Aaron’s family from generation to generation. That is why it is described here as an enduring priesthood.
Did you know? The Torah gives the Tabernacle’s opening date precisely: the first day of Nisan, in the second year after the Exodus.
Did you know? “The Testimony” placed in the Ark refers to the tablets of the covenant, so called because they testify to the covenant between God and Israel.
Did you know? Leviticus explains that the bread of the Presence consisted of twelve loaves, which the priests replaced every Sabbath.
Did you know? Inside the Tabernacle, the menorah had a fixed place on the south side and the table on the north side. This created an organized layout for the sacred space.
Did you know? The words “Moses completed the work” echo the ending of the creation story in Genesis. This creates a parallel between building the Tabernacle and creating the world.
Did you know? The cloud and the fire served as a visible signal for all Israel: when the cloud lifted, they traveled; when it remained over the Tabernacle, they stayed.
